Yet beings wrongly reckon right and wrong, and forcibly give rise to quarrels and disputes—altogether like those two men, with no difference.

〔65 · The Five Hundred Joy Pills〕（0552c13）Once there was a woman, wanton and without restraint; since her lust was so strong, she hated and loathed her husband, constantly thought of schemes, and planned to do him harm; she tried all kinds of plots, but never got her chance. It happened that her husband was sent on an embassy to a neighboring country; the woman secretly made a plan and made poison pills, wishing to use them to kill her husband, and deceitfully said to him: “Now you are going far away on an embassy, and I worry that you will run short of things; now I have made five hundred joy pills, to give you as provisions for the road. When you have left the country and reached another land, eat them only when you are hungry and worn.” The husband followed her words; after he had reached the other land, before he had had time to eat them, in the dark of night he stopped to spend the night in a forest, and fearing wild beasts, he climbed a tree to escape them, forgetting the joy pills at the foot of the tree. That very night, five hundred thieves, who had stolen five hundred horses and treasures from the king of that country, came and rested beneath the tree; because they had been fleeing, all of them were hungry and thirsty, and beneath the tree they saw the joy pills; the thieves took them and each ate one pill; the poison of the pills was fierce, and the five hundred thieves all died at once. When daybreak came, the man in the tree saw this band of thieves lying dead beneath the tree, and, making a pretense, slashed the corpses with his sword and shot them with arrows, gathered up their saddled horses and treasures, and drove them toward that country. At that time the king of that country, leading a great many men, came in pursuit following the tracks, and midway along the road the man came upon that king. That king asked him: “Who are you? Where did you get these horses?” The man answered: “I am a man of such-and-such a country; on the road I came upon this band of thieves, and we slashed and shot at one another; the five hundred thieves now all lie dead in one place, beneath the tree. For this reason I have got these horses and treasures, and have come to take refuge in the great king’s country. If you do not believe me, you may send someone to go and look at the thieves’ wounds and the place where they were killed.” The king at once sent a trusted man to go and look, and it was just as he had said. The king was then delighted and exclaimed that such a thing had never been; after returning to his country, he generously bestowed rank and rewards on him, gave him great treasures, and enfeoffed him with villages. That king’s old ministers all grew jealous and said to the king: “He is a man from afar, and cannot yet be trusted; how can you suddenly favor him so excessively, so that his rank and rewards surpass those of the old ministers?” The man from afar, having heard this, said: “Who is brave and strong enough to test himself against me? I ask to compete in skill on the open plain.” The old ministers were all astonished, and none dared oppose him. Later, in a great wilderness of that country, there was a fierce lion that blocked the road and killed people, cutting off the king’s road. At that time the old ministers deliberated together carefully: “That man from afar thinks himself brave and strong, with no one able to match him; if now he can also kill that lion and rid the country of harm, that will truly be remarkable.” Having deliberated thus, they reported it to the king; the king, having heard it, gave him a sword and staff and at once sent him off. Then the man from afar, having received the command, steeled his will and went toward the lion. The lion saw him, roused itself in fury, roared, and leapt forward; the man from afar, terrified, at once climbed a tree. The lion opened its mouth and raised its head toward the tree; the man, in fear and haste, let slip the sword he was holding, which fell right into the lion’s mouth, and the lion at once died. Then the man from afar, jumping for joy, came and reported to the king; the king favored him twice as much, and at that time the people of that country all at once respected and submitted to him, and all praised him.

The woman’s joy pills stand for impure giving; the king sending an envoy stands for a good friend; going to another country stands for the gods; killing the band of thieves stands for attaining stream-entry and forcibly cutting off the five desires and all the afflictions; meeting that king stands for encountering the worthy and noble ones. The old people of the country growing jealous stands for the followers of other paths, who, seeing that the wise can cut off the afflictions and the five desires, then give rise to slander and say there is no such thing. The man from afar saying, to provoke them, that none of the old ministers could match him stands for no one among the followers of other paths daring to resist and clash with him. Killing the lion stands for defeating Māra. Having cut off the afflictions and also subdued the evil Māra, one then obtains the fruit of the Way of non-attachment as fief and reward. Always being timid and afraid stands for being able to overcome the strong by the weak. Though at the beginning he had no pure mind, yet that one act of giving of his met with a good friend, and he obtained a superior reward; if impure giving is still like this, how much more so giving joyfully with a good mind? Therefore one should, in the field of merit, diligently cultivate giving.

〔66 · Reciting the Art of Steering a Boat Without Knowing How to Use It〕（0553b26）Once there was the son of a great elder who went to sea together with a number of merchants to gather treasure. This son of the elder was very good at reciting the methods of handling a ship at sea: that if one entered places in the sea where the water whirls in eddies and back-currents and the swift flow dashes against the rocks, one should hold it thus, set it right thus, and keep it steady thus. He said to the people: “The methods of going to sea, I know them all.” Having heard this, the people deeply believed his words. When they had reached the middle of the sea, before much time had passed, the helmsman fell ill and suddenly died. Then the son of the elder took the helmsman’s place, and in the midst of the whirling eddies and swift currents he sang out: “One should hold it thus, set it right thus.” But the ship spun round and round and could not go forward to reach the place of treasure, and all the merchants on the ship sank into the water and died.

Ordinary people are so too: having studied a little the methods of meditation, the counting of breaths in ānāpāna, and the contemplation of impurity, though they recite the texts, they do not understand their meaning; of all the various methods they in truth know nothing, yet they claim to understand them well; they wrongly teach the methods of meditation, causing those who follow them to be confused and lose their minds, and they turn the marks of the Dharma upside down; year after year they gain nothing at all—just like that fool who caused others to sink in the sea.

〔67 · The Husband and Wife Who Made a Wager over a Cake〕（0553c11）Once there were a husband and wife who had three cakes. The two shared them out, each eating one cake, and one was left over; so the two together made a pact, saying: “If either of us speaks, by our pact that one shall not get the cake.” Once the pact was made, for the sake of one cake neither dared to speak. Before long a thief entered the house to steal and took their goods; everything they had fell into the thief’s hands; because of their earlier pact, husband and wife watched with open eyes and did not speak. The thief, seeing that they did not speak, assaulted the wife in front of her husband, and the husband watched and still did not speak. The wife then cried out that there was a thief, and said to her husband: “How can there be a fool like you, who for the sake of one cake sees a thief and does not cry out?” The husband clapped his hands, laughed, and said: “Ha, you slave girl! I have surely won the cake; I will not give it to you.” Of the people of the world who heard of this, there was none who did not jeer.

Ordinary people are so too: for the sake of a little fame and gain, they make a false show of silence, and are assailed and plundered by the false afflictions, all kinds of evil thieves; they lose their good dharmas and fall into the three evil destinies, yet are not afraid at all and do not seek the world-transcending Way, but instead indulge in play amid the five desires; though they meet with great suffering, they do not think it a calamity—altogether like that fool, with no difference.

〔68 · Harming Each Other out of Hatred〕（0553c26）Once there was a man who bore hatred toward another and was sorrowful and unhappy. Someone asked him: “Why are you now so sorrowful and haggard?” He answered: “Someone has insulted me, and my strength is not enough to repay him; I do not know by what means I could repay him, and so I am sorrowful.” Someone said to him: “Only the vetāla spell can harm him; but there is one danger: before it has had time to harm him, it will harm you yourself first.” Having heard this, the man was overjoyed: “Only teach it to me; though it will harm me, still I hope to wound him.”

People of the world are so too: for the sake of anger they wish to seek the vetāla spell, to use it to afflict the other; in the end they do not harm the other, but first, through anger, afflict and harm themselves instead, and fall into hell, among the animals and the hungry ghosts—altogether like that fool, with no difference.

〔69 · Eating Fast in Imitation of His Ancestors〕（0554a08）Once there was a man who came from North India to South India; after he had lived there a long time, he married the daughter of a family there, and they became husband and wife. Then the wife prepared food and drink for her husband, and the husband, getting it, gulped it down in haste, not minding that it was hot. The wife at that time found this strange and said to her husband: “There are no robbers here who plunder people; what urgent business is there, that you are in such a hurry and cannot eat calmly and slowly?” The husband answered his wife: “There is a good secret matter that I cannot tell you.” The wife, hearing his words, thought there was some extraordinary method, and pressed him earnestly with questions; after a long while he answered: “From my grandfather’s time on, the family way has always been to eat fast; I now follow it, and so I eat fast.”

Ordinary people of the world are so too: they do not penetrate the right principle and do not know good and evil; they commit all kinds of wrong conduct and are not ashamed of it, and yet say that from their grandfathers’ time on they have followed such a way; until death they keep practicing it and never give it up—just like that fool, who was used to his fast eating and thought it a good way.

〔70 · Tasting the Āmra Fruit〕（0554a20）Once there was an elder who sent a man with money to another’s orchard to buy āmra fruit, wishing to eat it, and instructed him: “Buy only the good, sweet ones.” The man took the money and went to buy the fruit. The owner of the fruit said: “The fruit of these trees of mine are all fine, without a single bad one; taste one fruit, and that is enough to know.” The man buying the fruit said: “I must now taste them one by one, and only then take them; if I taste only one, how can I know?” He at once picked up the fruit and tasted every one of them, one by one, and carried them home. The elder, seeing this, was disgusted and would not eat them, and threw them all away.

People of the world are so too: they hear that keeping the precepts and giving bring great wealth and happiness, and that the body is always at peace, without any calamities, yet they are unwilling to believe it, and say: “That giving brings merit—when I myself get it, then I can believe it.” They see with their own eyes that in this present life the noble and the base, the poor and the destitute, are all the fruition and retribution obtained from deeds of former lives, yet they do not know to infer from one thing in order to seek cause and effect; instead they harbor disbelief and must experience it in their own persons; once life ends, their goods are lost—just like that man who tasted the fruit, and everything was thrown away.

〔71 · Losing Both Eyes on Account of Two Wives〕（0554b05）Once there was a man who took two wives: if he drew near to one, he was resented by the other. Unable to decide, he lay down on his back, his body straight, between the two wives. It happened that a great rain fell from the sky and the house leaked; water and mud fell down together into his eyes; because of an earlier agreement, he dared not get up to avoid it, and so both his eyes lost their sight.

Ordinary people of the world are so too: they draw near to wrong friends, practice what is not in accord with the Dharma, create karma that binds, fall into the three evil paths, dwell long in birth and death, and lose the eye of wisdom—just like that foolish man who, for the sake of his two wives, lost both eyes.

〔72 · The Mouthful of Rice and the Cut Cheek〕（0554b13）Once there was a man who went to his wife’s family home, saw them pounding rice, went over to the place, stole some rice, and held it in his mouth. His wife came, saw her husband, and wished to speak with him; his mouth full of rice, he made no answer at all; ashamed before his wife, he would not spit out the rice, and so he did not speak. His wife, finding it strange that he did not speak, felt with her hand and thought his mouth was swollen, and said to her father: “My husband has just arrived and has suddenly come down with a swollen mouth; he cannot speak at all.” Her father then called a physician to treat him. Then the physician said: “This illness is most grave; if it is cut open with a knife, it can be cured.” And he cut open his mouth with a knife; the rice came out from inside, and the matter was laid bare.

People of the world are so too: they commit all kinds of evil conduct and violate the pure precepts, conceal their faults and are unwilling to bring them to light, and fall into hell, among the animals and the hungry ghosts. They are like that fool who, because of a little shame, would not spit out the rice, until his mouth was cut open with a knife, and only then was his fault revealed.

〔73 · Falsely Claiming the Horse Had Died〕（0554b25）Once there was a man who rode a black horse into battle to strike at the enemy; because he was afraid, he could not fight, and so he smeared his face with blood, made a false show of being dead, and lay among the dead, and the horse he rode was taken by someone else. After the troops had gone, he wished to go home, and so he cut off the tail of another man’s white horse and brought it with him. When he got home, someone asked him: “Where is the horse you rode now? Why are you not riding it?” He answered: “My horse is already dead, so I brought its tail back.” A bystander said to him: “Your horse was black to begin with; how is its tail white?” He was silent, with no answer to give, and was laughed at by people.

People of the world are so too: they say of themselves that they are very good, that they cultivate a mind of kindness and do not take wine or meat; yet they kill and harm living beings and inflict all kinds of torments on them; falsely they call themselves good, while in truth there is no evil they do not do—just like that fool who falsely claimed his horse had died.

〔74 · The Renunciant Who Craved Gain and Offerings〕（0554c07）Once there was a king who set up an edict: whatever brāhmaṇas and others there were within my kingdom were all ordered to wash themselves clean; those who did not wash clean were driven and put to work at all kinds of hard labor. There was a brāhmaṇa who held an empty washing jug and falsely said that he washed himself clean; when people poured water in for him, he at once poured it away. And he said: “I do not wash clean; the king washes it himself.” In order to satisfy the king’s will and so escape the king’s labor service, he falsely said that he washed clean, while in truth he did not wash.

Ordinary people who have left home are so too: they shave their heads and put on dyed robes, while within they in truth break the precepts; they make a false show of keeping the precepts, hoping to get gain and offerings, and also escape the king’s labor service; outwardly they seem to be ascetics, while within they are in truth false and deceitful—just like holding an empty bottle, which has only an outward form.

〔75 · Losing Both the Camel and the Jar〕（0554c17）Once there was a man who had first stored grain in a jar; a camel put its head into the jar to eat the grain and then could not get it out; since it could not get out, the man was worried and distressed about it. An old man came and said to him: “Do not worry! I will teach you how to get it out. If you follow my words, it will surely come out quickly: you should cut off its head, and it will come out of itself.” The man followed his words and cut off the camel’s head with a knife, so that he both killed the camel and broke the jar. A fool like this is laughed at by the world.

Ordinary foolish people are so too: in their hearts they hope for bodhi and set their minds on seeking the three vehicles; they ought to keep the precepts and guard against all evils; yet for the sake of the five desires they break the pure precepts; once they have violated the precepts, they abandon the three vehicles, give free rein to their minds and follow their every wish, and there is no evil they do not do; the three vehicles and the pure precepts, both together are cast away—just like that fool who lost both the camel and the jar.

〔76 · The Farmer Who Pined for the Princess〕（0554c28）Once there was a farmer who went strolling in a city and saw the king’s daughter, her countenance comely, rare in the world; day and night he thought of her, and his longing could not stop; he wished to have relations with her but had no way to bring it about; his face turned sallow, and he fell gravely ill. His relatives all saw this and asked him: “Why are you like this?” He answered his kin: “Yesterday I saw the king’s daughter, her countenance comely; I wish to have relations with her and cannot, and so I am ill. If I do not get her, I shall surely die.” His relatives said to him: “We will find a good means for you, to let you have her; do not worry.” Some days later they saw him and said to him: “We have managed this for you, and it can be counted as done; only the king’s daughter is unwilling.” The farmer, hearing this, laughed gladly, thinking he was sure to get her.

The fools of the world are so too: they do not distinguish the seasons, spring, autumn, winter, and summer, and in winter they throw seed into the soil, hoping to get fruit; they waste their effort in vain and gain nothing at all; sprouts, stems, branches, and leaves—all are lost. The fools of the world cultivate a little merit and think it complete, and then think that bodhi can already be realized—just like that farmer who hoped for the king’s daughter.

〔77 · Milking the Donkey〕（0555a14）Once the people of a border country did not know the donkey; they heard others say that donkey’s milk was very sweet and fine, but none of them knew it. At that time the people got a male donkey and, wishing to milk it, fought with one another to catch hold of it: among them, some caught hold of its head, some of its ears, some of its tail, some of its legs, and others again held a vessel, each wishing to get the milk first and drink it in front of the rest. One of them caught hold of the donkey’s member, thinking that this was the milk, and milked it, hoping to get milk. The people were tired and weary, all of them got nothing, toiled for nothing and gained nothing at all, and were jeered at by all the people of the world.

Ordinary people among the followers of other paths are so too: hearing talk of the Way, they wrongly give rise to notions in places where it should not be sought, give rise to all kinds of wrong views, go naked, starve themselves, throw themselves from cliffs and leap into fire; because of these wrong views they fall into the evil paths—just like that fool who wrongly sought milk.

〔78 · Telling His Son to Set Out Early〕（0555a25）Once there was a man who said to his son at night: “Tomorrow I will go with you to that village; there is something to fetch.” The son heard this, and when morning came, without asking his father at all, went there alone. When he had got there, his body was utterly exhausted and he gained nothing at all; he also got no food, so that he was nearly dying of hunger and thirst; he soon came back again and came to see his father. The father, seeing his son return, rebuked him sharply: “You are very foolish and without wisdom; why did you not wait for me? You went there and back for nothing and suffered this hardship in vain, and you are jeered at by all the people of the world.”

Ordinary people are so too: if they are able to leave home, they shave off beard and hair and put on the three Dharma robes, yet they do not seek an enlightened teacher to consult and receive from him the Dharma of the Way; they lose all meditation, the factors of the path, and merit, and the wondrous fruit of the ascetic—all of it is lost—just like that fool who went there and back for nothing, wearing himself out in vain; in form they look like ascetics, but in truth they gain nothing.

〔79 · Carrying the King’s Stool〕（0555b08）Once there was a king who wished to go into the Garden Without Sorrow to enjoy himself, and instructed a minister: “Take a stool and bring it to that garden; I will use it to sit and rest.” Then that envoy, ashamed to carry it in his hands, would not take it, and reported to the king: “I cannot carry it in my hands; I would rather carry it on my back.” Then the king put thirty-six stools on his back and drove him to carry them to the garden. A fool like this is laughed at by the world.

Ordinary people are so too: if they see a single hair of a woman on the ground, they say of themselves that they keep the precepts and will not pick it up; later, deluded by the afflictions, they do not think the thirty-six things—hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, excrement and urine, and the other impure things—to be ugly; the thirty-six things they take up all at once, without feeling shame and remorse, and do not give them up until death—just like that fool who carried the stools on his back.

〔80 · The Enema Taken the Wrong Way〕（0555b19）Once there was a man who suffered from an illness of the lower parts. The physician said: “You must take an enema; then you can be cured.” And the equipment for the enema was gathered, so as to give it to him. Before the physician had arrived, the man took it and swallowed it, and his belly swelled until he was nearly dying, unable to bear it. When the physician arrived, he found this strange and asked him: “Why are you like this?” He answered the physician: “The enema medicine just now—I took it and swallowed it, and so I am nearly dying.” The physician, hearing this, rebuked him sharply: “You are a very foolish man, who does not understand means.” He then gave him other medicine to swallow, and only then did he vomit and purge, and so he was cured. A fool like this is laughed at by the world.

Ordinary people are so too: wishing to cultivate and learn the various methods of meditative contemplation, where they should learn the impure, they instead learn the counting of breaths; where they should count the breaths, they learn to contemplate the six elements; they turn high and low upside down and have no root; they waste their lives in vain and are trapped by it. Not consulting a good teacher, they turn the methods of meditation upside down—just like that fool who drank and swallowed what was impure.

〔81 · Bitten by a Bear〕（0555c03）Once there were a father and son walking together with companions; the son went into a forest and was bitten by a bear, its claws tearing his body; in distress and danger he came out of the forest and returned to his companions. The father, seeing his son’s body wounded, asked him in surprise: “Why have you now received such wounds?” The son told his father: “There is a kind of creature, the hair of its body long and shaggy, that came and wounded me.” The father took his bow and arrows and went into the forest, where he saw a sage whose hair was thick and long, and wished to shoot him. A bystander said to him: “Why shoot him? This man does no harm; you should punish the one at fault.”

The fools of the world are so too: abused and insulted by those who, though they wear the Dharma robes, have no practice of the Way, they wrongly harm good and virtuous people—just like that father, whose son was wounded by a bear, but who wrongly inflicted harm on a divine sage.

〔82 · Imitating the Sowing of a Field〕（0555c13）Once there was a rustic who came to the fields and saw fine wheat sprouts growing thick and lush, and asked the owner of the wheat: “How can one make this wheat grow so lush and fine?” The owner of the wheat answered: “Level the ground and add manure and water as well; that is how it comes to be like this.” The man then applied this method: he mixed water and manure into his field and sowed seed in the ground. He was afraid that his own feet would tread the ground and make it hard, and then the wheat would not grow: “I should sit on a couch and have people carry it, and scatter the seed from above; that will be good.” He then had four men each lift one leg of the couch and went to the field to scatter seed; the ground was trodden harder than ever, and he was jeered at by people: afraid of his own two feet, he instead added eight more.

Ordinary people are so too: having already tilled the field of the precepts, when good sprouts are about to come forth, they ought to consult their teachers and elders and receive and practice their instruction and admonition, so that the sprouts of the Dharma may grow; yet instead they violate it and do many evil things, and so they keep the sprouts of the precepts from growing—just like that man who, afraid of his two feet, instead added eight.
〔83 · The Monkey〕（0555c26）Once there was a monkey that was beaten by a grown man; able to do nothing against the grown man, it bore a grudge instead against a little child.

Ordinary foolish people are so too: the person they were angry with before has already passed away and been replaced without pause, perishing into the past; yet they take the dharmas that arise afterward in continuity to be that former person, wrongly give rise to angry resentment, and their venomous rage grows ever deeper—just like that foolish monkey which, beaten by the grown man, turned its anger instead on the little child.

〔84 · Beating the Dog for the Eclipse of the Moon〕（0556a03）Once the asura king, seeing the sun and the moon bright and clear, covered them with his hand; and common folk without wisdom wrongly inflict cruel blows on a dog that has done nothing wrong.

Ordinary people are so too: through greed, anger, and folly, they wrongly torment their own bodies, lying on thorns and scorching the body with the five fires—just like wrongly and needlessly beating the dog at the time of the eclipse of the moon.

〔85 · The Woman with Aching Eyes〕（0556a08）Once there was a woman whose eyes were in great pain. A woman she knew asked her: “Are your eyes in pain?” She answered: “My eyes are in pain.” That woman she knew said again: “Having eyes, one is sure to have pain; though mine are not yet in pain, I too wish to gouge out my eyes, for fear they will hurt later.” A bystander said to her: “If the eyes are still there, they may hurt or may not hurt; if the eyes are gone, there is lasting pain all one’s life.”

The foolish and ordinary are so too: hearing that wealth and rank are the root of decline and calamity, they are afraid and will not give, fearing that later they will receive the reward, their goods will overflow, and they will again undergo suffering and vexation. Someone said to them: “If you give, there may be suffering or there may be happiness; if you do not give, there will be poverty and great suffering.” They are like that woman who, unable to bear the pain close at hand, wished to get rid of her eyes, and so it became lasting pain instead.

〔86 · The Father Who Took His Son’s Earrings〕（0556a17）Once there were a father and son who, on account of some business, set out together; on the road robbers suddenly appeared and were about to come and strip them. The son had earrings of real gold in his ears; his father, seeing the robbers suddenly coming and afraid of losing the earrings, pulled at them with his hand; the ears would not tear off at once, and for the sake of the earrings he cut off his son’s head. A moment later the robbers left them and went away; he put his son’s head back on his shoulders, but could not restore it as before. A fool like this is laughed at by the world.

Ordinary people are so too: for the sake of fame and gain they engage in idle play, saying that the two worlds exist and that the two worlds do not exist, that the intermediate existence exists and that the intermediate existence does not exist, that mental factors exist and that mental factors do not exist—all kinds of false thinking—and they do not attain the reality of the Dharma. When others refute what they have argued with arguments in accord with the Dharma, they say: “In my treatise there is no such statement at all.” Fools like this, for the sake of a little fame and gain, deliberately speak falsely and lose the fruits of the Way of the ascetic; when the body breaks up and life ends, they fall into the three evil paths—just like that fool who, for a little gain, cut off his son’s head.

〔87 · The Robbers Dividing Their Loot〕（0556b01）Once there was a band of robbers who went raiding together and seized a great deal of goods; they then divided it together, making equal shares; only one deer-park kambala, its color not pure and fine, they made into the lowest share and gave to the meanest of them. The lowly one, getting it, was angry and resentful, thinking he had suffered a great loss, and took it to the city to sell. Many noble elders offered a high price for it, so that what this one man got was double what his companions got, and only then was he overjoyed beyond measure.

It is like people of the world who do not know whether giving has a reward or has no reward, and practice a little giving, and are reborn in the heavens and enjoy measureless happiness, and only then are they regretful, regretting that they did not give widely at first. Just as with that kambala, which later fetched a great price, and only then was joy brought forth, so giving too: doing little, one gains much, and only then does one congratulate oneself, sorry not to have done more.

〔88 · The Monkey with a Fistful of Beans〕（0556b11）Once there was a monkey holding a handful of beans; by mistake it dropped one bean on the ground, and then threw away the beans in its hand, wishing to look for that one; before it had found that one bean, the ones it had thrown away before had all been eaten up by chickens and ducks.

Ordinary people who leave home are so too: at first they break one precept and cannot repent; because they do not repent, heedlessness grows and spreads, and everything is abandoned—just like that monkey, which lost one bean and threw everything away.

〔89 · Finding a Golden Weasel〕（0556b17）Once there was a man walking along the road who found on the way a golden weasel; his heart leapt with joy, and he took it and put it in the fold of his robe and went on along the road; when he came to water and wished to cross, he took off his clothes and put them on the ground, and at once the golden weasel turned into a poisonous snake. This man thought deeply: “I would rather be stung to death by the poisonous snake; still I must carry it with me in my robe.” His intention was utterly sincere, and there was a hidden response: it changed back into gold. Beside him was a foolish man who, seeing the poisonous snake turn into a true treasure, thought it was always so, and in turn caught a poisonous snake and put it in the fold of his own robe, and was at once stung by the poisonous snake, losing his body and his life.

The fools of the world are so too: they see that doing good brings gain, yet within they have no true mind; only for the sake of gain and offerings do they come and attach themselves to the Dharma; after life ends they fall into an evil place—just like the man who caught the poisonous snake, was stung, and died.

〔90 · Finding Gold Coins on the Ground〕（0556b27）Once there was a poor man walking along the road who happened to find on the way a bag of gold coins; his heart leapt with great joy, and he at once began to count the coins; before he had counted them through once, the owner of the gold suddenly arrived and took all the coins back. At that time the man regretted not having left quickly, and his vexation was extremely painful.

Those who meet the Buddha’s Dharma are so too: though they have been able to meet the Three Jewels, the field of merit, they do not diligently practice means and cultivate good deeds; suddenly their life ends and they fall into the three evil paths—just like that fool, whose coins were taken back again by their owner. Just as a verse says:
Today they manage this affair, tomorrow they make that deed;
attached to pleasure, they do not see suffering, nor perceive the thief that is death arriving.
In haste they manage their many tasks; of ordinary people there is none who is not so,
like that man who counted the coins; this matter too is just so.

〔91 · The Poor Man Who Wanted Wealth Equal to the Rich〕（0556c10）Once there was a poor man who had a few goods; seeing a very rich man, he wished in his heart to be equal to him; because he could not be equal, though he had a few goods, he wished to throw them into the water. A bystander said to him: “Though these things are few, they can still prolong your life for some days; why throw them away and cast them into the water?”

The fools of the world are so too: though they have been able to leave home and have obtained a little gain and offerings, they have hopes in their hearts and always feel unsatisfied, unable to be equal to those of high virtue and to obtain gain and offerings like theirs. Seeing others, elders of long standing who are virtuous, who have long had much learning and receive offerings from many, they wish in their hearts to be equal to them; because they cannot be equal, they harbor sorrow in their hearts and wish to give up the Way, abandoning the way of one who has left home—just like that fool who wished to be equal to the rich man and threw away his own goods.

〔92 · The Child Who Got a Joy Pill〕（0556c20）Once there was a nurse carrying a child along the road; worn out on the way, she fell asleep without knowing it. Then a man gave the child a joy pill; the child, getting it, craved its fine taste and paid no heed to the things on its body; this man at once undid the child’s neck ring and lock, its necklaces, and its clothing, and took them all away.

Bhikṣus are so too: they delight in being in places of many affairs and bustle, crave a little gain and offerings, and are robbed by the thieves of the afflictions of their merit, the jewel of the precepts, and their necklaces—just like that child who, because it craved a little fine taste, had everything it had taken away by the thief.

〔93 · The Old Woman Who Caught a Bear〕（0556c28）Once there was an old woman lying beneath a tree, and a bear wished to come and seize her; at that time the old woman ran round the tree to escape it, and the bear chased after her, embracing the tree with one paw, trying to catch the old woman. The old woman, in desperate straits, at once wrapped her arms around the tree and pressed down the bear’s two paws, so that the bear could not move. Then another man came to the place, and the old woman said to him: “Catch it together with me, and we will kill it and share its meat.” Then that man believed the old woman’s words and at once caught hold of it with her. Once they had caught it, the old woman let go of the bear and ran off, and the man was afterward trapped by the bear. A fool like this is laughed at by the world.

Ordinary people are so too: they compose all kinds of divergent treatises, which are not good, wordy and heavy in style, with many faults, and in the end never finished; they set them aside and die; later people take them up, wishing to explain them, but do not penetrate their meaning, and are trapped by them instead—just like that fool who caught the bear for another and was himself harmed instead.

〔94 · Maṇi and the Water Drain〕（0557a11）Once there was a man who had relations with another man’s wife; before they had finished, the husband came back from outside and at once discovered it; he waited outside the door, watching for the moment the man came out, intending to kill him. The woman said to the man: “My husband has already discovered us; there is no other way out; only by the maṇi can you get out (in the Qi tongue, maṇi means a drain-hole).” She wished the man to get out through the water drain. The man misunderstood, taking it to be a maṇi jewel; he searched for it everywhere but did not know where it was, and said: “If I do not see the maṇi jewel, I will never leave.” A moment later he was killed by the husband.

Ordinary people are so too: someone said to them: “Within birth and death there is impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and no-self; leave the two extremes of annihilation and permanence and abide in the middle way; passing through by this middle, one can attain liberation.” The ordinary people misunderstood and sought instead whether the world is bounded or boundless, and whether beings have a self or have no self; in the end they cannot contemplate the principle of the middle way; suddenly their life ends, and they are killed by impermanence and fall into the three evil paths—just like that fool who searched for the maṇi and was killed by another.

〔95 · The Two Pigeons〕（0557a25）Once there were two pigeons, a male and a female, living together in one nest; in autumn, when the fruit was ripe, they gathered fruit and filled the nest; after that, the fruit dried and shrank, and only half a nest was left. The male pigeon grew angry and said to the female: “Gathering the fruit was hard toil, and you have eaten it alone; only half is left.” The female pigeon answered: “I did not eat it alone; the fruit shrank of itself.” The male pigeon did not believe her, and said angrily: “If you did not eat it alone, how could it have shrunk?” And he pecked the female pigeon with his beak and killed her. Not many days later, a great rain fell from the sky; the fruit was moistened and became as it had been before. The male pigeon, seeing this, only then felt regret: “She truly did not eat it; I killed her wrongly.” And crying mournfully, he called to the female pigeon, asking where she had gone.

Ordinary people are so too: inverted views lodge in their minds; they wrongly grasp at the pleasures of desire and do not contemplate impermanence; they violate the grave prohibitions, and only afterward regret it—yet what good can that do? Afterward there is only lamenting, just like that foolish pigeon.

〔96 · Feigning Blindness〕（0557b08）Once there was a craftsman who worked for the king and could not bear the hardship; he falsely said that his eyes were blind, and so was able to escape the hardship. Another workman heard of it and wished to ruin his own eyes, to escape the hard labor. Someone said to him: “Why do you harm yourself? You will only suffer this pain for nothing.” A fool like this is laughed at by the people of the world.

Ordinary people are so too: for the sake of a little reputation and gain and offerings, they deliberately speak falsely and ruin the pure precepts; when the body dies and life ends, they fall into the three evil paths—just like that fool who, for a little gain, ruined his own eyes.

〔97 · Robbed of His Fine Cotton by Bandits〕（0557b16）Once there were two men who, as companions, crossed a wilderness together; one of them wore a length of fine cotton cloth, and midway along the road he was stripped of it by bandits; the other fled and ran into the grass. The man who lost the fine cotton cloth had earlier wrapped a gold coin in one end of the cloth, and he said to the bandits: “This garment is worth exactly one gold coin; I now ask to redeem it with one gold coin.” The bandits said: “Where is the gold coin now?” He at once untied it from the end of the cloth, took it out and showed it to them, and said to the bandits: “This is real gold; if you do not believe my words, there is now in this grass a good goldsmith; you can go and ask him.” The bandits, having seen that man, took his clothes as well. A fool like this lost both the fine cotton cloth and the gold coin, everything; he lost his own gain and made the other lose too.

Ordinary people are so too: they cultivate the factors of the path and do all kinds of merit, but are plundered by the thieves of the afflictions, lose their good dharmas, and lose all their merit; not only do they lose their own gain, they also make other people lose their work of the Way; when the body breaks up and life ends, they fall into the three evil paths—just like that fool, through whom both the one and the other lost.

〔98 · The Child Who Caught a Great Tortoise〕（0557c01）Once there was a child playing on dry land who found a great tortoise; he wished to kill it but did not know how, and asked someone: “How can I kill it?” Someone said to him: “Just throw it into the water, and it can be killed at once.” Then the child believed his words and threw the tortoise into the water; the tortoise, having got to the water, at once went off.

Ordinary people are so too: wishing to guard the six sense faculties and cultivate all kinds of merit, but not understanding means, they ask someone: “By doing what causes and conditions can one attain liberation?” Followers of other paths with wrong views, the heavenly Māra Pāpīyān, and bad friends say to them: “Just indulge yourself to the utmost in the six sense objects and give free rein to the five desires; those who do as I say will surely attain liberation.” Fools like this, not reflecting carefully, follow their words; when the body breaks up and life ends, they fall into the three evil paths—just like that child who threw the tortoise into the water.

1. In the Northern Ocean there is a fish, the name of which is Khwän 2,--I do not know how many lî in size. It changes into a bird with the name of Phing, the back of which is (also)--I do not know how many lî in extent. When this bird rouses itself and flies, its wings are like clouds all round the sky. When the sea is moved (so as to bear it along), it prepares to remove to the Southern Ocean. The Southern Ocean is the Pool of Heaven.

There is the (book called) Khî Hsieh 1,--a record of marvels. We have in it these words:--'When the phäng is removing to the Southern Ocean it flaps (its wings) on the water for 3000 lî. Then it ascends on a whirlwind 90,000 lî, and it rests only at the end of six months.' (But similar to this is the movement of the breezes which we call) the horses of the fields, of the dust (which quivers in the sunbeams), and of living things as they are blown against one another by the air 2. Is its azure the proper colour of the sky? Or is it occasioned by its distance and illimitable extent? If one were looking down (from above), the very same appearance would just meet his view.

2. And moreover, (to speak of) the accumulation of water;--if it be not great, it will not have strength to support a large boat. Upset a cup of water in a cavity, and a straw will float on it as if it were a boat. Place a cup in it, and it will stick fast;--the water is shallow and the boat is large. (So it is with) the accumulation of wind; if it be not great, it will not have strength to support great wings. Therefore (the phäng ascended to) the height of 90,000 lî, and there was such a mass of wind beneath it; thenceforth the accumulation of wind was sufficient. As it seemed to bear the blue sky on its back, and there was nothing to obstruct or arrest its course, it could pursue its way to the South.

A cicada and a little dove laughed at it, saying, 'We make an effort and fly towards an elm or sapan-wood tree; and sometimes before we reach it, we can do no more but drop to the ground. Of what use is it for this (creature) to rise 90,000 lî, and make for the South?' He who goes to the grassy suburbs 1, returning to the third meal (of the day), will have his belly as full as when he set out; he who goes to a distance of 100 lî will have to pound his grain where he stops for the night; he who goes a thousand lî, will have to carry with him provisions for three months. What should these two small creatures know about the matter? The knowledge of that which is small does not reach to that which is great; (the experience of) a few years does not reach to that of many. How do we know that it is so? The mushroom of a morning does not know (what takes place between) the beginning and end of a month; the short-lived cicada does not know (what takes place between) the spring and autumn. These are instances of a short term of life. In the south of Khû 2, there is the (tree) called Ming-ling 3, whose spring is 500 years, and its autumn the same; in high antiquity there was that called Tâ-khun 4,

whose spring was 8000 years, and its autumn the same. And Phäng Zû 1 is the one man renowned to the present day for his length of life:--if all men were (to wish) to match him, would they not be miserable?

3. In the questions put by Thang 2 to Kî we have similar statements:--'In the bare and barren north there is the dark and vast ocean,--the Pool of Heaven. In it there is a fish, several thousand lî in breadth, while no one knows its length. Its name is the khwän. There is (also) a bird named the phäng; its back is like the Thâi mountain, while its wings are like clouds all round the sky. On a whirlwind it mounts upwards as on the whorls of a goat's horn for 90,000 lî, till, far removed from the cloudy vapours, it bears on its back the blue sky, and then it shapes its course for the South, and proceeds to the ocean there.' A quail by the side of a marsh laughed at it, and said, 'Where is it going to? I spring up with a bound, and come down again when I have reached but a few fathoms, and then fly about among the brushwood and bushes; and
this is the perfection of flying. Where is that creature going to?' This shows the difference between the small and the great.

Thus it is that men, whose wisdom is sufficient for the duties of some one office, or whose conduct will secure harmony in some one district, or whose virtue is befitting a ruler so that they could efficiently govern some one state, are sure to look on themselves in this manner (like the quail), and yet Yung-dze 1 of Sung 1 would have smiled and laughed at them. (This Yung-dze), though the whole world should have praised him, would not for that have stimulated himself to greater endeavour, and though the whole world should have condemned him, would not have exercised any more repression of his course; so fixed was he in the difference between the internal (judgment of himself) and the external (judgment of others), so distinctly had he marked out the bounding limit of glory and disgrace. Here, however, he stopped. His place in the world indeed had become indifferent to him, but still he had not planted himself firmly (in the right position).
There was Lieh-dze 2, who rode on the wind and pursued his way, with an admirable indifference (to

all external things), returning, however, after fifteen days, (to his place). In regard to the things that (are supposed to) contribute to happiness, he was free from all endeavours to obtain them; but though he had not to walk, there was still something for which he had to wait. But suppose one who mounts on (the ether of) heaven and earth in its normal operation, and drives along the six elemental energies of the changing (seasons), thus enjoying himself in the illimitable,--what has he to wait for'? Therefore it is said, 'The Perfect man has no (thought of) self; the Spirit-like man, none of merit; the Sagely-minded man, none of fame 1.'

4. Yâo 2, proposing to resign the throne to Hsü Yû 3, said, 'When the sun and moon have come forth, if the torches have not been put out, would it not be difficult for them to give light? When the seasonal rains are coming down, if we still keep watering the ground, will not our toil be labour lost for all the good it will do? Do you, Master, stand forth (as sovereign), and the kingdom will (at once) be well governed. If I still (continue to) preside over it, I must look on myself as vainly occupying the place;--I beg to resign the throne to you.' Hsü

[paragraph continues] Yû said, 'You, Sir, govern the kingdom, and the kingdom is well governed. If I in these circumstances take your place, shall I not be doing so for the sake of the name? But the name is but the guest of the reality;--shall I be playing the part of the guest? The tailor-bird makes its nest in the deep forest, but only uses a single branch; the mole 1 drinks from the Ho, but only takes what fills its belly. Return and rest in being ruler,--I will have nothing to do with the throne. Though the cook were not attending to his kitchen, the representative of the dead and the officer of prayer would not leave their cups and stands to take his place.'

5. Kien Wû 2 asked Lien Shû 2, saying, 'I heard Khieh-yû 3 talking words which were great, but had nothing corresponding to them (in reality);-once gone, they could not be brought back. I was frightened by them;--they were like the Milky Way 4 which cannot be traced to its beginning or end. They had no connexion with one another, and were not akin to the experiences of men.' 'What were his words?' asked Lien Shift, and the other replied, (He said) that 'Far away on the hill of Kû-shih 5 there dwelt a Spirit-like man whose flesh and skin

were (smooth) as ice and (white) as snow; that his manner was elegant and delicate as that of a virgin; that he did not eat any of the five grains, but inhaled the wind and drank the dew; that he mounted on the clouds, drove along the flying dragons, rambling and enjoying himself beyond the four seas; that by the concentration of his spirit-like powers he could save men from disease and pestilence, and secure every year a plentiful harvest.' These words appeared to me wild and incoherent and I did not believe them. 'So it is,' said Lien Shû. 'The blind have no perception of the beauty of elegant figures, nor the deaf of the sound of bells and drums. But is it only the bodily senses of which deafness and blindness can be predicated? There is also a similar defect in the intelligence; and of this your words supply an illustration in yourself. That man, with those attributes, though all things were one mass of confusion, and he heard in that condition the whole world crying out to him to be rectified, would not have to address himself laboriously to the task, as if it were his business to rectify the world. Nothing could hurt that man; the greatest floods, reaching to the sky, could not drown him, nor would he feel the fervour of the greatest heats melting metals and stones till they flowed, and scorching all the ground and hills. From the dust and chaff of himself, he could still mould and fashion Yâos and Shuns 1;how should he be willing to occupy himself with things 2?'

6. A man of Sung, who dealt in the ceremonial caps (of Yin) 1, went with them to Yüeh 2, the people of which cut off their hair and tattooed their bodies, so that they had no use for them. Yâo ruled the people of the kingdom, and maintained a perfect government within the four seas. Having gone to see the four (Perfect) Ones 3 on the distant hill of Kû-shih, when (he returned to his capital) on the south of the Fän water 4, his throne appeared no more to his deep-sunk oblivious eyes 5.

7. Hui-dze 6 told Kwang-dze, saying, 'The king of Wei 7 sent me some seeds of a large calabash, which I sowed. The fruit, when fully grown, could contain five piculs (of anything). I used it to contain water,

but it was so heavy that I could not lift it by myself. I cut it in two to make the parts into drinking vessels; but the dried shells were too wide and unstable and would not hold (the liquor); nothing but large useless things! Because of their uselessness I knocked them to pieces.' Kwang-dze replied, 'You were indeed stupid, my master, in the use of what was large. There was a man of Sung who was skilful at making a salve which kept the hands from getting chapped; and (his family) for generations had made the bleaching of cocoon-silk their business. A stranger heard of it, and proposed to buy the art of the preparation for a hundred ounces of silver. The kindred all came together, and considered the proposal. "We have," said they, "been bleaching cocoon-silk for generations, and have only gained a little money. Now in one morning we can sell to this man our art for a hundred ounces;--let him have it." The stranger accordingly got it and went away with it to give counsel to the king of Wû 1, who was then engaged in hostilities with Yüeh. The king gave him the command of his fleet, and in the winter he had an engagement with that of Yüeh, on which he inflicted a great defeat 2, and was invested with a portion of territory taken from Yüeh. The keeping the hands from getting chapped was the same in both cases; but in the one case it led to the investiture (of the possessor of the salve), and

in the other it had only enabled its owners to continue their bleaching. The difference of result was owing to the different use made of the art. Now you, Sir, had calabashes large enough to hold five piculs;--why did you not think of making large bottle-gourds of them, by means of which you could have floated over rivers and lakes, instead of giving yourself the sorrow of finding that they were useless for holding anything. Your mind, my master, would seem to have been closed against all intelligence!'

Hui-dze said to Kwang-dze, 'I have a large tree, which men call the Ailantus 1. Its trunk swells out to a large size, but is not fit for a carpenter to apply his line to it; its smaller branches are knotted and crooked, so that the disk and square cannot be used on them. Though planted on the wayside, a builder would not turn his head to look at it. Now your words, Sir, are great, but of no use;--all unite in putting them away from them.' Kwang-dze replied, 'Have you never seen a wildcat or a weasel? There it lies, crouching and low, till the wanderer approaches; east and west it leaps about, avoiding neither what is high nor what is low, till it is caught in a trap, or dies in a net. Again there is the Yak 2, so large that it is like a cloud hanging in the sky. It is large indeed, but it cannot catch mice. You, Sir, have a large tree and are troubled because it is of no use;--why do you not plant it in a tract where there is nothing else, or in a wide and barren wild?

[paragraph continues] There you might saunter idly by its side, or in the enjoyment of untroubled case sleep beneath it. Neither bill nor axe would shorten its existence; there would be nothing to injure it. What is there in its uselessness to cause you distress?'

1. Nan-kwo Sze-khî 2 was seated, leaning forward on his stool. He was looking up to heaven and breathed gently, seeming to be in a trance, and to have lost all consciousness of any companion. (His disciple), Yen Khäng Dze-yû 3, who was in attendance and standing before him, said, 'What is this? Can the body be made to become thus like a withered tree, and the mind to become like slaked lime? His appearance as he leans forward on the stool to-day is such as I never saw him have before in the same position.' Dze-khî said, 'Yen, you do well to ask such a question, I had just now lost myself 4; but how should you understand it? You
may have heard the notes 1 of Man, but have not heard those of Earth; you may have heard the notes of Earth, but have not heard those of Heaven.'

Dze-yû said, 'I venture to ask from you a description of all these.' The reply was, 'When the breath of the Great Mass (of nature) comes strongly, it is called Wind. Sometimes it does not come so; but when it does, then from a myriad apertures there issues its excited noise;--have you not heard it in a prolonged gale? Take the projecting bluff of a mountain forest;--in the great trees, a hundred spans round, the apertures and cavities are like the nostrils, or the mouth, or the ears; now square, now round like a cup or a mortar; here like a wet footprint, and there like a large puddle. (The sounds issuing from them are like) those of fretted water, of the arrowy whizz, of the stern command, of the inhaling of the breath, of the shout, of the gruff note, of the deep wail, of the sad and piping note. The first notes are slight, and those that follow deeper, but in harmony with them. Gentle winds produce a small response; violent winds a great one. When the fierce gusts have passed away, all the apertures
are empty (and still);--have you not seen this in the bending and quivering of the branches and leaves?'

Dze-yû said, 'The notes of Earth then are simply those which come from its myriad apertures; and the notes of Man may just be compared to those which (are brought from the tubes of) bamboo;--allow me to ask about the notes of Heaven 1.' Dze-khî replied, 'When (the wind) blows, (the sounds from) the myriad apertures are different, and (its cessation) makes them stop of themselves. Both of these things arise from (the wind and the apertures) themselves:--should there be any other agency that excites them?'

2. Great knowledge is wide and comprehensive; small knowledge is partial and restricted. Great speech is exact and complete; small speech is (merely) so much talk 2. When we sleep, the soul communicates with (what is external to us); when we awake, the body is set free. Our intercourse with others then leads to various activity, and daily there is the striving of mind with mind. There are hesitancies; deep difficulties; reservations; small apprehensions causing restless distress, and great

apprehensions producing endless fears. Where their utterances are like arrows from a bow, we have those who feel it their charge to pronounce what is right and what is wrong.; where they are given out like the conditions of a covenant, we have those who maintain their views, determined to overcome. (The weakness of their arguments), like the decay (of things) in autumn and winter, shows the failing (of the minds of some) from day to day; or it is like their water which, once voided, cannot be gathered up again. Then their ideas seem as if fast bound with cords, showing that the mind is become like an old and dry moat, and that it is nigh to death, and cannot be restored to vigour and brightness.

Joy and anger, sadness and pleasure, anticipation and regret, fickleness and fixedness, vehemence and indolence, eagerness and tardiness;--(all these moods), like music from an empty tube, or mushrooms from the warm moisture, day and night succeed to one another and come before us, and we do not know whence they sprout. Let us stop! Let us stop! Can we expect to find out suddenly how they are produced?

If there were not (the views of) another, I should not have mine; if there were not I (with my views), his would be uncalled for:--this is nearly a true, statement of the case, but we do not know what it is that makes it be so. It might seem as if there would be a true Governor 1 concerned in it, but we do not find
any trace (of his presence and acting). That such an One could act so I believe; but we do not see His form. He has affections, but He has no form.

Given the body, with its hundred parts, its nine openings, and its six viscera, all complete in their places, which do I love the most? Do you love them all equally? or do you love some more than others? Is it not the case that they all perform the part of your servants and waiting women? All of them being such, are they not incompetent to rule one another? or do they take it in turns to be now ruler and now servants? There must be a true Ruler (among them) 1 whether by searching you can find out His character or not, there is neither advantage nor hurt, so far as the truth of His operation is concerned. When once we have received the bodily form complete, its parts do not fail to perform their functions till the end comes. In conflict with things or in harmony with them, they pursue their course to the end, with the speed of a galloping horse which cannot be stopped;--is it not sad? To be constantly toiling all one's lifetime, without seeing the fruit of one's labour, and to be weary and worn out with his labour, without knowing where he is going to:--is it not a deplorable case? Men may say, 'But it is not death;' yet of what advantage is this? When the body is decomposed, the mind will be the same along with it:--must not the case be pronounced very deplorable 2? Is the life
of man indeed enveloped in such darkness? Is it I alone to whom it appears so? And does it not appear to be so to other men?

3. If we were to follow the judgments of the predetermined mind, who would be left alone and without a teacher 1? Not only would it be so with those who know the sequences (of knowledge and feeling) and make their own selection among them, but it would be so as well with the stupid and unthinking. For one who has not this determined mind, to have his affirmations and negations is like the case described in the saying, 'He went to Yüeh to-day, and arrived at it yesterday 2.' It would be making what was not a fact to be a fact. But even the spirit-like Yü 3 could not have known how to do this, and how should one like me be able to do it?

But speech is not like the blowing (of the wind) the speaker has (a meaning in) his words. If, however, what he says, be indeterminate (as from a mind not made up), does he then really speak or not? He thinks that his words are different from the chirpings of fledgelings; but is there any distinction between them or not? But how can the Tâo be so obscured, that there should be 'a True' and 'a False' in it? How can speech be so obscured that there should be 'the Right' and 'the Wrong' about them? Where shall the Tâo go to that it will not

be found? Where shall speech be found that it will be inappropriate? Tâo becomes obscured through the small comprehension (of the mind), and speech comes to be obscure through the vain-gloriousness (of the speaker). So it is that we have the contentions between the Literati 1 and the Mohists 2, the one side affirming what the other denies, and vice versâ. If we would decide on their several affirmations and denials, no plan is like bringing the (proper) light (of the mind) 3 to bear on them.

All subjects may be looked at from (two points of view),--from that and from this. If I look at a thing from another's point of view, I do not see it; only as I know it myself, do I know it. Hence it is said, 'That view comes from this; and this view is a consequence of that:'--which is the theory that that view and this--(the opposite views)-produce each the other 4. Although it be so, there is affirmed now life and now death; now death and now life; now the admissibility of a thing and now its inadmissibility; now its inadmissibility and now its admissibility. (The disputants) now affirm and now deny; now deny and now affirm. Therefore the sagely man does not pursue this method, but views things in the light of (his) Heaven 5 (-ly nature), and hence forms his judgment of what is right.

This view is the same as that, and that view is the same as this. But that view involves both a right and a wrong; and this view involves also a right and a wrong:--are there indeed, or are there not the two views, that and this? They have not found their point of correspondency which is called the pivot of the Tâo. As soon as one finds this pivot, he stands in the centre of the ring (of thought), where he can respond without end to the changing views;--without end to those affirming, and without end to those denying. Therefore I said, 'There is nothing like the proper light (of the mind).'

4. By means of a finger (of my own) to illustrate that the finger (of another) is not a finger is not so good a plan as to illustrate that it is not so by means of what is (acknowledged to be) not a finger; and by means of (what I call) a horse to illustrate that (what another calls) a horse is not so, is not so good a plan as to illustrate that it is not a horse, by means of what is (acknowledged to be) not a horse 1. (All things in) heaven and earth may be (dealt with as) a finger; (each of) their myriads may be (dealt with as) a horse. Does a thing seem so to me? (I say that) it is so. Does it seem not so to me? (I say that) it is not so. A path is formed by (constant)

treading on the ground. A thing is called by its name through the (constant) application of the name to it. How is it so? It is so because it is so. How is it not so? It is not so, because it is not so. Everything has its inherent character and its proper capability. There is nothing which has not these. Therefore, this being so, if we take a stalk of grain 1 and a (large) pillar, a loathsome (leper) and (a beauty like) Hsî Shih 2, things large and things insecure, things crafty and things strange;--they may in the light of the Tâo all be reduced to the same category (of opinion about them).

It was separation that led to completion; from completion ensued dissolution. But all things, without regard to their completion and dissolution, may again be comprehended in their unity;--it is only the far reaching in thought who know how to comprehend them in this unity. This being so, let us give up our devotion to our own views, and occupy ourselves with the ordinary views. These ordinary views are grounded on the use of things. (The study of that) use leads to the comprehensive judgment, and that judgment secures the success (of the inquiry). That success gained, we are near (to the object of our search), and there we stop. When we stop, and yet we do not know how it is so, we have what is called the Tâo.
When we toil our spirits and intelligence, obstinately

determined (to establish our own view), and do not know the agreement (which underlies it and the views of others), we have what is called 'In the morning three.' What is meant by that 'In the morning three?' A keeper of monkeys, in giving them out their acorns, (once) said, 'In the morning I will give you three (measures) and in the evening four.' This made them all angry, and he said, 'Very well. In the morning I will give you four and in the evening three.' His two proposals were substantially the same, but the result of the one was to make the creatures angry, and of the other to make them pleased:--an illustration of the point I am insisting on. Therefore the sagely man brings together a dispute in its affirmations and denials, and rests in the equal fashioning of Heaven 1. Both sides of the question are admissible.

5. Among the men of old their knowledge reached the extreme point. What was that extreme point? Some held that at first there was not anything. This is the extreme point, the utmost point to which nothing can be added 2. A second class held that there was something, but without any responsive recognition 3 of it (on the part of men).
A third class held that there was such recognition, but there had not begun to be any expression of different opinions about it.

It was through the definite expression of different opinions about it that there ensued injury to (the doctrine of) the Tâo. It was this injury to the (doctrine of the) Tâo which led to the formation of (partial) preferences. Was it indeed after such preferences were formed that the injury came? or did the injury precede the rise of such preferences? If the injury arose after their formation, Kâo's method of playing on the lute was natural. If the injury arose before their formation, there would have been no such playing on the lute as Kâo's 1.

Kâo Wän's playing on the lute, Shih Kwang's indicating time with his staff, and Hui-dze's (giving his views), while leaning against a dryandra tree (were all extraordinary). The knowledge of the three men (in their several arts) was nearly perfect, and therefore they practised them to the end of their lives. They loved them because they were different from those of others. They loved them and wished to make them known to others. But as they could not be made clear, though they tried to make them so, they ended with the obscure (discussions) about 'the hard' and 'the White.' And their sons 2, moreover, with all the threads of their fathers' compositions, yet to the end of their lives accomplished nothing. If they, proceeding in this way, could be said to have succeeded, then am I also successful;
if they cannot be pronounced successful, neither I nor any other can succeed.

Therefore the scintillations of light from the midst of confusion and perplexity are indeed valued by the sagely man; but not to use one's own views and to take his position on the ordinary views is what is called using the (proper) light.

6. But here now are some other sayings 1:--I do not know whether they are of the same character as those which I have already given, or of a different character. Whether they be of the same character or not when looked at along with them, they have a character of their own, which cannot be distinguished from the others. But though this be the case, let me try to explain myself.
There was a beginning. There was a beginning before that beginning 2. There was a beginning previous to that beginning before there was the beginning.

There was existence; there had been no existence. There was no existence before the beginning of that no existence 2. There was no existence previous to the no existence before there was the beginning of the no existence. If suddenly there was nonexistence, we do not know whether it was really anything existing, or really not existing. Now I have said what I have said, but I do not know whether what I have said be really anything to the point or not.

Under heaven there is nothing greater than the tip of an autumn down, and the Thâi mountain is small. There is no one more long-lived than a child which dies prematurely, and Phäng Zû did not live out his time. Heaven, Earth, and I were produced together, and all things and I are one. Since they are one, can there be speech about them? But since they are spoken of as one, must there not be room for speech? One and Speech are two; two and one are three. Going on from this (in our enumeration), the most skilful reckoner cannot reach (the end of the necessary numbers), and how much less can ordinary people do so! Therefore from non-existence we proceed to existence till we arrive at three; proceeding from existence to existence, to how many should we reach? Let us abjure such procedure, and simply rest here 1.

7. The Tâo at first met with no responsive recognition. Speech at first had no constant forms of expression. Because of this there came the demarcations (of different views). Let me describe those demarcations:--they are the Left and the Right 2; the Relations and their Obligations 3; Classifications 4

and their Distinctions; Emulations and Contentions. These are what are called 'the Eight Qualities.' Outside the limits of the world of men 1, the sage occupies his thoughts, but does not discuss about anything; inside those limits he occupies his thoughts, but does not pass any judgments. In the Khun Khiû 2, which embraces the history of the former kings, the sage indicates his judgments, but does not argue (in vindication of them). Thus it is that he separates his characters from one another without appearing to do so, and argues without the form of argument. How does he do so? The sage cherishes his views in his own breast, while men generally state theirs argumentatively, to show them to others. Hence we have the saying, 'Disputation is a proof of not seeing clearly.'

The Great Tâo 3 does not admit of being praised. The Great Argument does not require words. Great Benevolence is not (officiously) benevolent. Great Disinterestedness does not vaunt its humility. Great Courage is not seen in stubborn bravery.

The Tâo that is displayed is not the Tâo. Words that are argumentative do not reach the point. Benevolence that is constantly exercised does not accomplish its object. Disinterestedness that vaunts its purity is not genuine. Courage that is most stubborn

is ineffectual. These five seem to be round (and complete), but they tend to become square (and immovable) 1. Therefore the knowledge that stops at what it does not know is the greatest. Who knows the argument that needs no words, and the Way that is not to be trodden 2?

He who is able to know this has what is called 'The Heavenly Treasure-house 3.' He may pour into it without its being filled; he may pour from it without its being exhausted; and all the while he does not know whence (the supply) comes. This is what is called 'The Store of Light 3.'

Therefore of old Yâo asked Shun, saying, 'I wish to smite (the rulers of) Zung, Kwei, and Hsü-âo 4. Even when standing in my court, I cannot get them out of my mind. How is it so?' Shun replied, 'Those three rulers live (in their little states) as if they were among the mugwort and other brushwood;--how is it that you cannot get them out of your mind? Formerly, ten suns came out together, and all things were illuminated by them;--how much should (your) virtue exceed (all) suns!'
8. Nieh Khüeh 5 asked Wang Î 5, saying, 'Do you know, Sir, what all creatures agree in approving and

affirming?' 'How should I know it?' was the reply. 'Do you know what it is that you do not know?' asked the other again, and he got the same reply. He asked a third time,--'Then are all creatures thus without knowledge?' and Wang Î answered as before, (adding however), 'Notwithstanding, I will try and explain my meaning. How do you know that when I say "I know it," I really (am showing that) I do not know it, and that when I say "I do not know it," I really am showing that I do know it 1.' And let me ask you some questions:--'If a man sleep in a damp place, he will have a pain in his loins, and half his body will be as if it were dead; but will it be so with an eel? If he be living in a tree, he will be frightened and all in a tremble; but will it be so with a monkey? And does any one of the three know his right place? Men eat animals that have been fed on grain and grass; deer feed on the thickset grass; centipedes enjoy small snakes; owls and crows delight in mice; but does any one of the four know the right taste? The dog-headed monkey finds its mate in the female gibbon; the elk and the axis deer cohabit; and the eel enjoys itself with other fishes. Mâo Zhiang 2 and Lî Kî 2 were accounted by men to be most beautiful, but when fishes saw them, they dived deep in the water from them; when birds, they flew from them aloft; and

when deer saw them, they separated and fled away 1. But did any of these four know which in the world is the right female attraction? As I look at the matter, the first principles of benevolence and righteousness and the paths of approval and disapproval are inextricably mixed and confused together:--how is it possible that I should know how to discriminate among them?'

Nieh Khüeh said (further), 'Since you, Sir, do not know what is advantageous and what is hurtful, is the Perfect man also in the same way without the knowledge of them?' Wang i replied, 'The Perfect man is spirit-like. Great lakes might be boiling about him, and he would not feel their heat; the Ho and the Han might be frozen up, and he would not feel the cold; the hurrying thunderbolts might split the mountains, and the wind shake the ocean, without being able to make him afraid. Being such, he mounts on the clouds of the air, rides on the sun and moon, and rambles at ease beyond the four seas. Neither death nor life makes any change in him, and how much less should the considerations of advantage and injury do so 2!'
9. Khü Zhiâo-dze 3 asked Khang-wû Dze 3, saying,

'I heard the Master (speaking of such language as the following):--"The sagely man does not occupy himself with worldly affairs. He does not put himself in the way of what is profitable, nor try to avoid what is hurtful; he has no pleasure in seeking (for anything from any one); he does not care to be found in (any established) Way; he speaks without speaking; he does not speak when he speaks; thus finding his enjoyment outside the dust and dirt (of the world)." The Master considered all this to be a shoreless flow of mere words, and I consider it to describe the course of the Mysterious Way.--What do you, Sir, think of it?' Khang-wû dze replied, 'The hearing of such words would have perplexed even Hwang-Tî, and how should Khiû be competent to understand them? And you, moreover, are too hasty in forming your estimate (of their meaning). You see the egg, and (immediately) look out for the cock (that is to be hatched from it); you see the bow, and (immediately) look out for the dove (that is to be brought down by it) being roasted. I will try to explain the thing to you in a rough way; do you in the same way listen to me.

'How could any one stand by the side of the sun and moon, and hold under his arm all space and all time? (Such language only means that the sagely man) keeps his mouth shut, and puts aside questions that are uncertain and dark; making his inferior capacities unite with him in honouring (the One Lord). Men in general bustle about and toil; the

sagely man seems stupid and to know nothing 1. He blends ten thousand years together in the one (conception of time); the myriad things all pursue their spontaneous course, and they are all before him as doing so.

'How do I know that the love of life is not a delusion? and that the dislike of death is not like a young person's losing his way, and not knowing that he is (really) going home? Lî Kî 2 was a daughter of the border Warden of Ai. When (the ruler of) the state of Zin first got possession of her, she wept till the tears wetted all the front of her dress. But when she came to the place of the king 3, shared with him his luxurious couch, and ate his grain-and-grass-fed meat, then she regretted that she had wept. How do I know that the dead do not repent of their former craving for life?

'Those who dream of (the pleasures of) drinking may in the morning wail and weep; those who dream of wailing and weeping may in the morning be going out to hunt. When they were dreaming they did not know it was a dream; in their dream they may even have tried to interpret it 4; but when they awoke they knew that it was a dream. And
